title: Comparative diagnostics
text: This comparison focuses on the trade-offs between direct estimation, area-level SAE, unit-level SAE, and poststratified unit-level SAE. The diagnostics compare the scale and smoothness of the estimates, agreement between methods, external validation residuals, uncertainty, and local residual structure used by the models.

title: Comparative diagnostics
text:
1 Method Trade-Offs








Method
Main input
Main trade-off




Direct
Survey-weighted area-time estimates
Preserves the survey design most directly, but sparse MSOA-year cells can be unstable or missing.


FH
Weighted direct estimates and sampling variances
Uses the survey design through the direct estimates, but inherits their sparsity and degenerate variance issues.


BHF
Respondent records with unit-level predictors
Uses individual outcomes directly, but the fitted likelihood does not use survey weights.


MRP Shallow
Respondent records plus age-sex population cells and contextual predictors
Adds population reweighting, but only over the available poststratification cells.


MRP Rich
Respondent records plus age-sex-car population cells
Gives the closest alignment between model predictors and population composition, but holds the 2021 poststratification structure across later waves.

title: Comparative diagnostics
text:
2 Estimate Scale and Smoothing
The distribution and rank plots show how much each method changes the spread of MSOA-year estimates. Direct estimates retain the most cell-level jaggedness, while the model-based approaches borrow strength across areas, years, predictors, or poststratification cells.

title: Comparative diagnostics
text:
3 Method Agreement
MRP Rich is used here as a modelling reference because it uses the fullest poststratification structure available in the workflow. It is not an external benchmark; disagreement with it indicates how much the other methods differ from the richest unit-level specification.

title: Comparative diagnostics
text:
4 External Validation Residuals
The validation benchmark is the Census bicycle-to-work share. It is related to frequent cycling for transport but does not measure the same target outcome, so the residuals should be read as a directional comparison rather than a direct accuracy test.

\text{obs} = \frac{\text{bicycle-to-work count}}{\text{total commuters}}
 
\text{residual} = \frac{\text{obs} - \text{estimate}}{\sqrt{estimate}}

title: Comparative diagnostics
text:
6 Spatial and Local Residual Effects
The area-effect maps show where the fitted models allocate remaining area-level variation after the fixed effects and temporal structure. Structured effects represent spatially smoothed residual patterns, while unstructured effects represent local deviations that are not strongly explained by adjacency.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Theory in brief



Let c index poststratification cells within area j and time t. The cells are defined by whichever population variables are available for poststratification. In a unit-level SAE with poststratification approach, a binary cycling outcome can be modelled at the respondent level as

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ijt}) \\
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{ijt}) &=
\alpha + z_{ijt}^{T}\beta + u_j + v_t .
\end{aligned}

where z_{ijt} is a vector of respondent-level predictors used to define or adjust the poststratification cells, \beta contains their coefficients, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The fitted model gives predicted cell means for the binary frequent-cycling indicator in each poststratification cell:

\hat{\pi}_{jtc}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,c).

The poststratification step combines those cell predictions with population counts N_{jtc} available or estimated for the same cells. Area-time estimates are then population-weighted averages of the cell predictions. 
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{MRP}}
=
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\pi}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}}.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of adults who cycle for transport frequently
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




SAE with poststratification (MRP) extends the unit-level SAE workflow by combining a respondent-level outcome model with a poststratification table describing the target population. For this estimand, we model the binary frequent-cycling indicator using age_band, sex, car_access, and spatial and temporal random effects. We then produce predicted cell means for each age_band x sex x car_access population cell and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates using population weights. Uncertainty is propagated by repeating this aggregation across posterior draws.
Here, the poststratification table is sourced from ONS UK Census 2021, giving the 2021 population count for each age_band x sex x car_access cell in each MSOA. For the 2023 and 2025 estimands, the model can still estimate different area-time outcomes through the temporal and spatial terms, but the poststratification weights are held fixed. This assumes that local demographic and car-access composition does not change across the survey years. In other words, N_{jtc} = N_{jc,2021} for all three waves.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
1 Prepare modelling and poststratification data
There are two inputs when performing unit-level SAE with poststratification:

poststrat_data, the population cells over which predictions are averaged.
model_data, the sampled respondent records used to fit the model.

It is essential for the unit-level predictors to be identical to the ones present in the poststratification table. Therefore, age is grouped into the same broad Census age bands and sex is also recoded as Male and Female.

  select(area_id, time_id, area_inla_id, time_inla_id)

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit binomial unit-level models to respondent records, then use them to predict area-time means. We specify three unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:



Model
Name
Specification




M1
+TempSpatial
Temporal RW1 plus BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M2
+Demographic
M1 plus age band and sex


M3
+CarAccess
M2 plus respondent car access




m1_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- update(m1_formula, . ~ . +
  age_band +
  sex
)

m3_formula <- update(m2_formula, . ~ . +
  car_access
)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula
)


fit_mrp_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = 1,
    data = model_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

mrp_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_mrp_model)

As before, we use WAIC as an initial model check. The fixed-effect table reports the selected model’s predictor terms providing a directional check on whether the modelled relationships are consistent with expected cycling patterns.

      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
) |>
  arrange(waic)

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
3 Poststratification with posterior draws
As with the previous model-based methods, the final MSOA-year estimates are obtained by aggregating predictions across posterior draws. The key difference is that the unit-level model is fitted to respondent records, so its predictions can still reflect the composition of the survey sample instead of the real-world population if left unadjusted as done in the previous method. Poststratification addresses this by evaluating the fitted model over known population groups and reweighting those predictions by population counts, so the final estimates are aligned with the target population structure.





The poststratification step uses posterior draws from the selected INLA fit to produce MSOA-year estimates. We first sample from the posterior and extract the fixed effects, spatial area effect, and temporal effect. We then rebuild the fitted model for every age_band x sex x car_access population cell, weight those cell predictions by pop_count, and summarise the resulting MSOA-year draws.






Note



Each posterior draw stores the fixed effects, spatial area effect, and temporal effect together in INLA’s latent vector. Fixed effects are labelled as term:1, while random effects are labelled as effect:index.



set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = mrp_final_fit
)

# Fixed-effect draw matrix
fixed_terms <- rownames(mrp_final_fit$summary.fixed)
fixed_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0(fixed_terms, ":1"), 1]),
    fixed_terms
  )
})

# Area-effect draw matrix
area_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids), 1]),
    area_ids
  )
})

# Time-effect draw matrix
time_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids), 1]),
    time_ids
  )
})

For each posterior draw, we rebuild the fitted model for every poststratification cell.

cell_draws <- sapply(seq_along(posterior_draws), \(draw_id) {
  fixed_part <- fixed_draws["(Intercept)", draw_id] +
    as.integer(poststrat_data$age_band == "25_34") * fixed_draws["age_band25_34", draw_id] +
    as.integer(poststrat_data$age_band == "35_49") * fixed_draws["age_band35_49", draw_id] +
    as.integer(poststrat_data$age_band == "50_64") * fixed_draws["age_band50_64", draw_id] +
    as.integer(poststrat_data$age_band == "65_plus") * fixed_draws["age_band65_plus", draw_id] +
    as.integer(poststrat_data$sex == "Female") * fixed_draws["sexFemale", draw_id] +
    poststrat_data$car_access * fixed_draws["car_access", draw_id]

  cell_log_odds <- fixed_part +
    area_draws[as.character(poststrat_data$area_inla_id), draw_id] +
    time_draws[as.character(poststrat_data$time_inla_id), draw_id]

  plogis(cell_log_odds)
})

We then apply the poststratification weights by multiplying each cell prediction by its population count and aggregating within each MSOA-year.

area_year_id <- paste(poststrat_data$area_id, poststrat_data$time_id, sep = "__")

weighted_sums <- rowsum(
  cell_draws * poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = area_year_id,
  reorder = FALSE
)

populations <- rowsum(
  poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = area_year_id,
  reorder = FALSE
)

area_year_draws <- weighted_sums / as.numeric(populations)

Finally, we summarise the MSOA-year draws into the final estimate, variance, and 95% credible interval.

mrp_summary <- tibble(
  area_year_id = rownames(area_year_draws),
  mrp_estimate = rowMeans(area_year_draws),
  mrp_variance = apply(area_year_draws, 1, var),
  mrp_lower = apply(area_year_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
  mrp_upper = apply(area_year_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
) |>
  mutate(mrp_ci_width = mrp_upper - mrp_lower) |>
  separate(area_year_id, into = c("area_id", "time_id"), sep = "__", convert = TRUE)

final_mrp_results <- domain_frame |>
  select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id) |>
  left_join(mrp_summary, by = c("area_id", "time_id"))

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
section: 4 Appendix: Enhance shallow poststratification with contextual predictors
text:
4 Appendix: Enhance shallow poststratification with contextual predictors
Sometimes the population table is available for every target year but only at a shallow cell grain. For example, ONS mid-year population estimates can give MSOA-year counts by age_band and sex, but not by car_access. In that setting we can still use MRP, but the model may only specify two unit-level predictors represented in the poststratification table.
Contextual predictors can still help explain between-area or between-year variation. Since these predictors vary by MSOA, not by respondent within an MSOA, this is weaker than having unit-level predictors and matching poststratification cells because they cannot represent how cycling behaviour differs between adults with and without car access inside the same age-sex cell.

In the modelling step, the model specification uses age_band and sex as the poststratification-cell predictors, and adds the contextual area predictors directly as fixed effect terms.

shallow_base_formula <- indicator ~
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

shallow_context_formula <- update(shallow_base_formula, . ~ . +
  age_band +
  sex +
  population_density +
  car_access_hhshare
)

shallow_context_fit <- inla(
  formula = shallow_context_formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = 1,
  data = shallow_model_data,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
)

The WAIC comparison suggests that contextual predictors add less to model performance than the richer specification with the unit-level car-access predictor. When survey microdata and poststratification data are available at compatible predictor grains, the richer specification is preferred.


Code
rich_shallow_waic <- bind_rows(
  model_waic |>
    filter(model == mrp_best_model) |>
    transmute(
      workflow = "Rich MRP",
      model = "Age + Sex + CarAccess",
      waic,
      eff_params
    ),
  tibble(
    workflow = "Shallow MRP",
    model = "Age + Sex (+Area context)",
    waic = shallow_context_fit$waic$waic,
    eff_params = shallow_context_fit$waic$p.eff
  )
) |>
  arrange(waic)

The shallow poststratification step weights the fitted cell predictions only by the age-sex population counts for each MSOA-year.


Code
set.seed(101)
shallow_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(
  n = 300,
  result = shallow_context_fit
)

shallow_fixed_terms <- rownames(shallow_context_fit$summary.fixed)
shallow_fixed_draws <- sapply(shallow_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0(shallow_fixed_terms, ":1"), 1]),
    shallow_fixed_terms
  )
})

shallow_area_draws <- sapply(shallow_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("area_inla_id:", area_ids), 1]),
    area_ids
  )
})

shallow_time_draws <- sapply(shallow_draws, \(draw) {
  setNames(
    as.numeric(draw$latent[paste0("time_inla_id:", time_ids), 1]),
    time_ids
  )
})




Code
shallow_cell_matrix <- model.matrix(
  ~ age_band + sex + population_density + car_access_hhshare,
  data = shallow_poststrat_data
)[, shallow_fixed_terms, drop = FALSE]

shallow_cell_draws <- sapply(seq_along(shallow_draws), \(draw_id) {
  shallow_cell_log_odds <- as.numeric(
    shallow_cell_matrix %*% shallow_fixed_draws[, draw_id]
  ) +
    shallow_area_draws[as.character(shallow_poststrat_data$area_inla_id), draw_id] +
    shallow_time_draws[as.character(shallow_poststrat_data$time_inla_id), draw_id]

  plogis(shallow_cell_log_odds)
})




Code
shallow_area_year_id <- paste(
  shallow_poststrat_data$area_id,
  shallow_poststrat_data$time_id,
  sep = "__"
)

shallow_weighted_sums <- rowsum(
  shallow_cell_draws * shallow_poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = shallow_area_year_id,
  reorder = FALSE
)
shallow_populations <- rowsum(
  shallow_poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = shallow_area_year_id,
  reorder = FALSE
)
shallow_area_year_draws <- shallow_weighted_sums / as.numeric(shallow_populations)




Code
shallow_summary <- tibble(
  area_year_id = rownames(shallow_area_year_draws),
  shallow_mrp_estimate = rowMeans(shallow_area_year_draws),
  shallow_mrp_variance = apply(shallow_area_year_draws, 1, var),
  shallow_mrp_lower = apply(shallow_area_year_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
  shallow_mrp_upper = apply(shallow_area_year_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
) |>
  mutate(shallow_mrp_ci_width = shallow_mrp_upper - shallow_mrp_lower) |>
  separate(area_year_id, into = c("area_id", "time_id"), sep = "__", convert = TRUE)

shallow_mrp_results <- domain_frame |>
  select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id) |>
  left_join(shallow_summary, by = c("area_id", "time_id"))

title: SAE Toolkit
text: This SAE toolkit shows how to adapt the SAE workflow to another survey, geography, or outcome by mapping the inputs to a common schema and running the workflow pages in sequence.

2. Prepare the input tables
The workflow expects a small set of linked tables. Area-time inputs use area_id and time_id; respondent-level survey inputs also use unit_id.

Domain frame
One row for every area-time cell that should receive an estimate. This table defines the target grid, including cells with no survey respondents, and stores the numeric indices used by INLA.



Column
Meaning

Area to estimate

Time period to estimate

Numeric area index for INLA

Numeric time index for INLA

Optional area or period labels for display





Spatial graph
Spatial random effects need an adjacency graph with the same area ordering as area_inla_id.



File
Meaning




*.adj
INLA adjacency graph, ordered by area_inla_id





Survey indicator and unit-level predictors (if applicable)
One row per respondent-period for the outcome being estimated, together with the survey design fields and unit-level predictors.







Column
Meaning




unit_id
Respondent identifier


area_id
Area assigned to the respondent


time_id
Survey period


indicator
Outcome used in estimation (binary or continuous)

Survey design weight for direct estimation


strata
Survey stratum for direct estimation, if available


predictors
Unit predictors (age, sex, car access, etc.) if applicable





Area predictors
One row per area, with predictors used to explain spatial differences in the outcome. These are used in area-level SAE and can also support unit-level SAE as area-level summaries or contextual predictors.



Column
Meaning

Area identifier

Predictors transformed for modelling

Predictors in original units for interpretation





Poststratification table
Used when model predictions are aggregated over population groups to produce the final estimate in the Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP) workflow. The population cells must match the categorical predictors used for poststratification.







Column
Meaning




area_id
Area identifier


time_id
Time period


population groups
Age, sex, household type, or other poststratification categories


pop_count
Population count for each cell

title: A practical guide to Spatio-temporal Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
Small area estimation for Urban Analytics

Urban researchers often need survey estimates at the scale where urban questions are asked: neighbourhoods, census blocks, transport zones, or other local units. These estimates may be used to compare places, monitor change over time, identify local inequalities, or link survey outcomes to area-level conditions. Most surveys are not designed for reliable estimation at every local geography and time period, so area-year cells can contain only a few respondents or none at all.
This guide sets out a workflow for choosing spatio-temporal Bayesian small area estimation (SAE) methods for urban analytics, with implementation in INLA.



Bayesian inference and INLA

Bayesian inference combines survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, neighbouring-area structure, year-to-year structure, and uncertainty from sparse cells in one estimation framework. Modelled estimates are returned as posterior distributions, which makes uncertainty explicit.
The examples use R-INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA provides deterministic approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models, usually much faster than MCMC for this workflow.



Navigating the guide

The guide covers SAE routes commonly used with urban survey and auxiliary datasets. Method choice depends on the outcome, survey information, auxiliary data, and available population structure.


Estimation setup
Direct estimation
Modelling: Area-level (Fay–Herriot)
Modelling: Unit-level (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
Modelling: SAE with poststratification (MRP)
Comparative diagnostics
Toolkit




Data

The worked data are synthetic datasets based on the National Survey for Wales. The maps and estimates are workflow outputs, not empirical findings about specific places in Wales. Auxiliary predictors, boundaries, and poststratification tables are derived from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), including ONS UK Census 2021. The synthetic dataset construction and preprocessing steps are described in the estimation setup.



About the project

The tutorial is part of the TRACK-UK project by the City Modelling Lab.
TRACK-UK develops spatial and statistical methods for analysing mobility patterns at fine geographic scales and assessing their implications for transport decarbonisation in the UK. The project works with academic, policy, and industry partners to produce evidence for transport and energy policy.
For questions about the tutorial, contact:

Shaun Hoang - University College London
Anna Freni-Sterrantino - The Alan Turing Institute
Esra Suel - University College London; University of Zurich
